# CFKS: CONTINUUM-FEATURE KERNEL PDE SOLVERS **ABSTRACT** Neural-network-based PDE solvers require architectural choices, particularly the number of layers and neurons per layer. Fixing a single Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) feature layer and taking the number of features to the continuum limit removes the need to prescribe a finite feature count or select individual feature centers, thereby reducing representation arbitrariness. Motivated by this principle, we introduce Continuum-Feature Kernel Solver (CFKS), a deterministic framework for PDEs obtained by analytically marginalizing a bounded continuum of Gaussian RBF features. CFKS works directly with the resulting continuum-feature mean kernel and its operator-applied counterparts, parameterized by prescribed Gaussian widths and bounded center distributions. For linear PDEs, CFKS leads to symmetric operator-kernel collocation systems with null-space enforcement of physical constraints. Nonlinear PDEs are addressed through linearized initialization and nonlinear least-squares residual minimization using analytical kernel derivatives and Jacobians. Residual-guided collocation enrichment and sequential space--time-slab marching provide additional resolution strategies, while prescribed multiscale kernel refinement helps resolve localized nonlinear structures. Finite-feature experiments confirm convergence of empirical value and operator Gram matrices toward their continuum counterparts. Numerical studies include oscillatory and multiscale ODEs, irregular- domain Poisson and biharmonic problems, singular perturbations, transient transport equations, and viscous Burgers’ equation. The results establish CFKS as a direct computational connection between finite Gaussian-RBF representations and continuum-feature kernel PDE solvers. s: `https://github.com/vikas-dwivedi-2022/CFKS\_s` ### 1 Introduction Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are increasingly used for forward and inverse partial differential equation (PDE) problems [1]. However, their practical performance depends on architectural choices, particularly the number of layers and neurons per layer, as well as optimization and collocation-point placement. A natural way to reduce this architectural arbitrariness is to consider a single-layer Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) representation and take the number of features to the continuum limit. When the corresponding feature expectation is available analytically, the resulting kernel eliminates the need to prescribe a finite feature count or select individual feature centers. The representation nevertheless remains parameterized by prescribed Gaussian widths and center distributions, which influence approximation accuracy and numerical conditioning. This motivates the development of meshfree PDE solvers that work directly with continuum-feature kernels rather than finite feature realizations. ∗Corresponding Author **Vikas Dwivedi**∗

A particularly relevant line of development begins with radial-basis-function (RBF) collocation. Kansa introduced meshfree PDE solvers based on finite RBF expansions with explicitly prescribed centers [2, 3]. Subsequent work provided approximation-theoretic foundations and clarified limitations of unsymmetric collocation systems [4, 5]. Symmetric and Hermite formulations subsequently incorporated differential and boundary operators directly into kernel collocation by applying the corresponding operators to both arguments of a positive-definite kernel, thereby constructing symmetric operator-based collocation matrices [6].

In parallel, Gaussian-process and neural-network theory established the correspondence between feature representations and kernels. Infinite-width neural models may converge to Gaussian processes [7], while Gaussian-process theory relates continuous basis-function representations to covariance kernels [8]. In such representations, a deterministic kernel can be constructed by averaging products of basis functions over a prescribed distribution of feature parameters. We refer to the resulting kernel as the _continuum-feature mean kernel_. Neither infinite-feature limits nor continuum Gaussian-basis representations are new in themselves. The question addressed in this work is how to evaluate the bounded Gaussian-RBF mean kernel and its differential-operator counterparts analytically and employ them directly in PDE solvers with prescribed physical constraints.

Random-feature methods exploit the converse direction by approximating this mean kernel using a finite sampled feature map [9]. This idea has been transferred to PDEs through random-feature methods that retain a finite randomized trial space and solve only for output coefficients [10]. More recent work has considered localized, high-order, and operator-aware variants, including residual-Christoffel sampling for finite operator-applied feature spaces [11] and analytic partition-of-unity constructions for high-order PDEs [12]. Kernel and Gaussian-process methods have likewise been applied directly to differential operators, probabilistic collocation, and structurally constrained boundary-value problems [13, 14, 15].

The present work connects these developments through _Continuum-Feature Kernel Solver (CFKS)_, based on the exact bounded mean kernel induced by a Gaussian RBF feature family. Unlike finite RBF representations, which require a prescribed number of features and their individual center locations, CFKS replaces the finite feature realization with analytical averaging over a prescribed distribution of centers. This produces a deterministic continuum-feature mean kernel, eliminating finite-feature sampling variability while retaining the Gaussian widths and center distributions as prescribed parameters.

An important property of this construction is that differential operators can be applied directly to the mean kernel. The resulting operator-applied kernels are equivalent to analytically averaging the products of the corresponding operator- applied Gaussian features. Consequently, the kernel matrices required for PDE collocation can be constructed without explicitly generating finite RBF features. For Gaussian RBFs with centers uniformly distributed over bounded intervals or boxes, the mean kernel admits a closed-form expression involving a squared-exponential factor and error-function terms that account for the bounded center support [8].

For linear PDEs, CFKS uses the continuum-feature mean kernel and its operator-applied counterparts to construct symmetric strong-form collocation systems. Boundary and initial conditions can be enforced through a null-space parameterization, separating the satisfaction of physical constraints from the interior PDE approximation. For nonlinear PDEs, analytical kernel derivatives enable direct evaluation of the nonlinear residual and its Jacobian. Linearized solves provide initialization for nonlinear least-squares residual minimization, while analytical trial-function parameterizations can enforce the prescribed physical conditions. Problems exhibiting localized structures can be addressed through multiscale continuum-feature kernels and residual-guided collocation enrichment. These extensions are demonstrated using viscous Burgers’ equation with a two-stage predictor–corrector strategy.

## Research gap

Despite substantial developments in RBF collocation, kernel methods, Gaussian-process formulations, and random-feature PDE solvers, two methodological gaps motivate the present work:

• Finite RBF and random-feature PDE methods generally require a prescribed number of features and an explicit realization of their centers, whereas conventional kernel collocation typically starts from a prescribed kernel. Although continuum-feature limits are well established, the direct construction of PDE solvers from analytically marginalized bounded Gaussian-RBF feature distributions, including the corresponding differential-operator kernels, remains comparatively underexplored. Such a formulation removes the finite feature count and individual center selection while retaining prescribed Gaussian widths and center distributions.<tbc>

• The enforcement of boundary and initial conditions remains an important consideration in meshfree PDE solvers. Physical constraints are frequently incorporated through penalty terms, weighted least-squares formulations, or jointly assembled constraint systems. Although null-space methods for enforcing linear constraints are well established [16, 17, 18], their integration with analytically derived continuum-feature<tbc>

operator kernels, together with analytical constraint embeddings for nonlinear problems, provides a unified approach for separating the enforcement of physical conditions from the approximation of the governing PDE.

### Contributions

The main contributions of this work are:

• We develop CFKS by analytically replacing a finite Gaussian-RBF feature representation with its exact bounded continuum-feature mean kernel. This removes the need to prescribe a finite feature count or select individual feature centers, while retaining Gaussian widths and center distributions as prescribed parameters.<tbc>

• We derive the corresponding differential-operator kernels and employ them in symmetric strong-form collocation for linear PDEs. Boundary and initial conditions are enforced through a null-space parameterization, allowing the governing equations to be solved within a constraint-compatible subspace.<tbc>

• We extend CFKS to nonlinear PDEs through linearized initialization and nonlinear least-squares residual minimization, using analytical kernel derivatives and Jacobians. Analytical constraint embeddings and multiscale continuum-feature kernels further accommodate prescribed physical conditions and localized solution structures.<tbc>

• We integrate optional residual-adaptive collocation and sequential space-time-slab marching into the CFKS framework. Residual-guided enrichment concentrates computational resolution in regions of under-resolution, while prescribed multiscale kernel refinement provides additional flexibility for resolving localized structures.

Residual-based adaptive sampling is already well established in meshfree and physics-informed methods \[19, 20\]. In CFKS, it is incorporated as an optional refinement strategy in which independently evaluated PDE residuals guide the allocation of additional collocation points. When the mean kernel is fixed, this refinement changes the collocation and represententer sites without altering the underlying continuum-feature kernel or prescribed physical conditions. For nonlinear problems, collocation enrichment can additionally be combined with prescribed changes in kernel scales. Sequential space-time-slab marching extends this strategy to time-dependent problems, consistent with earlier time-marching and causality-aware formulations \[21, 22\].

### Organization of the paper

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the mathematical formulation of CFKS, including the continuum-feature mean kernel, operator-based collocation, constraint enforcement, and extensions to nonlinear PDEs, residual-adaptive collocation, and sequential space-time slabs. Section 3 introduces the numerical benchmark problems. Section 4 presents and discusses the numerical results, including finite-feature convergence and conditioning studies. Section 5 summarizes the main findings and outlines directions for future research. The appendices provide the connection between finite-feature models and the CFKS representer formulation, together with the analytical derivation of the bounded Gaussian continuum-feature kernel.

## 2 Mathematical tion

We first develop CFKS for linear differential problems and subsequently describe its extension to nonlinear PDEs. Let \(\Omega\) denote the computational domain and **z** the vector of independent variables. For time-dependent problems, **z**=(**x**_,t_), where **x** represents the spatial coordinates and _t_ denotes time. We consider the linear differential problem

\(\mathcal{L}u(\mathbf{z})=f(\mathbf{z}),\mathbf{z}\in\Omega,\) (1)

where L is a prescribed linear differential operator, _u_ is the unknown solution, and _f_ is a known source function. The problem is supplemented by boundary conditions and, for time-dependent equations, appropriate initial conditions.

To formulate the numerical problem, the governing PDE and its physical conditions are expressed through a collection of linear constraint functionals,

\(\ell_i[u]=y_i,i=1,\dots,N,\) (2)

where _N_ is the total number of discrete constraints, \(\ell_i\) denotes the linear functional associated with constraint _i_, and _y<sub>i</sub>_ is its prescribed value. For an interior PDE constraint imposed at a collocation point **z**_<sub>i</sub>_, the functional \(\ell_i\) applies the differential operator L to the solution at that point, with _y<sub>i</sub>=f_(**z**_<sub>i</sub>_). Boundary and initial conditions are represented by the corresponding evaluation or differential functionals at the selected physical constraint locations.

### 2.1 From finite RBF features to the continuum-feature mean kernel

We begin with a finite representation of the unknown solution using Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) features. Let **z**=(_z_<sub>1</sub>_,...,z<sub>d</sub>_) denote a point in the computational domain, where _d_ is the number of independent variables. For time-dependent problems, these variables include both spatial coordinates and time.

The _m_th Gaussian RBF feature is defined as \(\phi_{\theta_m}(\mathbf{z})=\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{r=1}^d\frac{(z_r-\theta_{m,r})^2}{\sigma_r^2}\right),\) (3) where \(\theta_m=(\theta_{m,1},\dots,\theta_{m,d})\) denotes the center of the _m_th feature, \(\theta_{m,r}\) is its center coordinate in the _r_th direction, and \(\sigma_r>0\) is the prescribed Gaussian width associated with that direction. The index _r_ runs over the _d_ independent variables. Equal widths in all directions give the isotropic Gaussian RBF, whereas different widths allow coordinate-dependent scaling. In space-time problems, separate spatial and temporal widths can therefore be prescribed. Using _M_ such features, where _M_ is the total number of Gaussian RBF features, the finite-feature approximation is expressed as \(u_M(\mathbf{z})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\sum_{m=1}^M\beta_m\phi_{\theta_m}(\mathbf{z}),\) (4) where _uM_ denotes the approximate solution, _m_ indexes the individual features, and \(\beta_m\) is the output coefficient associated with the _m_th feature. The feature centers and Gaussian widths are fixed when determining the coefficients from the governing constraints. The normalization factor \(1/\sqrt{M}\) ensures that the associated feature Gram matrix has a nontrivial finite limit as the number of features increases. Recall that the governing PDE and physical conditions are represented by _N_ linear constraint functionals, denoted by \(\ell_i\), with _i_=1_,...,N_. Applying these functionals to the finite-feature representation gives the constraint matrix _Z_, whose entries are \(Z_{im}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\ell_i[\phi_{\theta_m}],\) (5) where _Zim_ is the entry associated with constraint _i_ and feature _m_. Thus, _Z_ is an \(N\times M\) matrix, and \(\ell_i[\phi_{\theta_m}]\) denotes the result of applying the _i_th linear constraint functional to the _m_th Gaussian RBF feature. The corresponding constraint Gram matrix is obtained by multiplying _Z_ by its transpose: \((ZZ^\top)_{ij}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^M\ell_i[\phi_{\theta_m}]\ell_j[\phi_{\theta_m}],\) (6) where \(Z^\top\) denotes the transpose of _Z_, and _i,j_=1_,...,N_ index pairs of constraint functionals. The matrix \(ZZ^\top\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite, with each entry representing the inner product of two constraint-applied finite-feature vectors. To obtain the continuum-feature formulation, suppose that the Gaussian RBF centers are independently sampled from a prescribed probability distribution with density \(\rho(\theta)\), where \(\theta\) represents a generic feature-center vector. The distribution specifies the region and relative weighting of admissible feature centers. In the present work, bounded uniform center distributions are used. Rather than retaining an explicit finite realization of these centers, we consider the analytical mean of the products of Gaussian RBF features. This defines the _continuum-feature mean kernel_ \(k_\rho(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}')=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim\rho}\left[\phi_\theta(\mathbf{z})\phi_\theta(\mathbf{z}')\right],\) (7) where \(k_\rho\) denotes the mean kernel associated with the center distribution \(\rho\), and **z** and \(\mathbf{z}'\) are its first and second arguments, respectively. The notation \(\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim\rho}\) denotes expectation with respect to the prescribed probability distribution of the feature-center vector \(\theta\). The function \(\phi_\theta\) is the Gaussian RBF defined in eq. 3, with the generic center \(\theta\) replacing the individual center \(\theta_m\). For independently sampled feature centers, the law of large numbers implies that, as the number of features _M_ tends to infinity, each entry of the empirical constraint Gram matrix converges to its corresponding population value, provided the relevant feature moments are finite. For the bounded Gaussian-feature construction considered here, these conditions are satisfied. Consequently, \((ZZ^\top)_{ij}\longrightarrow\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim\rho}\left[\ell_i[\phi_\theta]\ell_j[\phi_\theta]\right]\)
\(=\ell_i^\mathbf{z}\ell_j^{\mathbf{z}^\prime} k_\rho(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}'),\) (8) where the superscripts on the constraint functionals identify the kernel argument on which each functional acts. Specifically, \(\ell_i^\mathbf{z}\) acts on the first argument of the kernel, while \(\ell_j^{\mathbf{z}^\prime}\) acts on the second. Each functional includes the appropriate differential or evaluation operation at the location associated with its constraint.

Equation 8 establishes that the continuum-feature constraint Gram matrix is the analytical expectation of the corresponding finite-feature Gram matrix. Thus, CFKS replaces the finite feature count and individual center realization with a deterministic kernel defined by the prescribed center distribution and Gaussian widths.

For Gaussian RBF features with centers uniformly distributed over bounded intervals, the expectation defining the continuum-feature mean kernel can be evaluated analytically. In one dimension, the resulting expression consists of a Gaussian factor multiplied by error-function terms that account for the finite support of the center distribution. When the center distribution is a product of independent uniform distributions over a Cartesian box, the multidimensional mean kernel is obtained as the product of the corresponding one-dimensional kernels. The complete derivation and closed-form expressions are provided in Appendix B.

An important property of the continuum-feature mean kernel is that its derivatives can be obtained directly from the analytical kernel expression. To describe derivatives of arbitrary order, let **_p_**=(_p_<sub>1</sub>_,...,p<sub>d</sub>_) and **_q_**=(_q_<sub>1</sub>_,...,q<sub>d</sub>_) denote two multi-indices, where _p<sub>r</sub>_ and _q<sub>r</sub>_ are nonnegative integers specifying the orders of partial differentiation with respect to the _r_th coordinates of **z** and \(\mathbf{z}'\), respectively. The operators \(D_\mathbf{z}^\mathbf{p}\) and \(D_{\mathbf{z}^\prime}^\mathbf{q}\) denote the corresponding mixed partial derivatives with respect to the first and second kernel arguments.

For the smooth Gaussian features and bounded center distributions considered here, differentiation can be interchanged with expectation. Therefore,

\(D_\mathbf{z}^\mathbf{p}D_{\mathbf{z}^\prime}^\mathbf{q}k_\rho(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}')=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim\rho}\left[D_\mathbf{z}^\mathbf{p}\phi_\theta(\mathbf{z})D_{\mathbf{z}^\prime}^\mathbf{q}\phi_\theta(\mathbf{z}')\right],\) (9)

which shows that the mixed derivatives of the mean kernel are equal to the analytical averages of the corresponding products of differentiated Gaussian RBF features.

In particular, for the prescribed linear differential operator L appearing in the governing PDE,

\(\mathcal{L}_\mathbf{z}\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{z}^\prime} k_\rho(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}')=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim\rho}\left[(\mathcal{L}\phi_\theta)(\mathbf{z})(\mathcal{L}\phi_\theta)(\mathbf{z}')\right],\) (10)

where L**<sub>z</sub>** and \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathbf{z}^\prime}\) indicate application of the differential operator to the first and second kernel arguments, respectively. On the right-hand side, \((\mathcal{L}\phi_\theta)(\mathbf{z})\) denotes the operator applied to a Gaussian RBF feature and evaluated at **z**, with the analogous interpretation for the second argument.

Equation 10 establishes that the operator-applied mean kernel is exactly the population Gram kernel associated with the corresponding operator-applied Gaussian RBF features. Hence, the differential-operator kernels required by CFKS follow directly from the continuum-feature construction rather than being introduced independently.

## 2.2 Linear CFKS formulation

We now construct the CFKS approximation for the linear differential problem introduced in eq. 1. Recall that \(\ell_i\), with _i_=1_,...,N_, denotes the linear functional associated with the _i_th governing PDE, boundary, or initial constraint, and _N_ is the total number of discrete constraints. Each functional includes the appropriate differential or evaluation operation at its prescribed constraint location.

Let \(k_\rho\) denote the continuum-feature mean kernel defined in eq. 7. The CFKS approximation is expressed in the kernel representer form

\(u_h(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_j\ell_j^{\mathbf{z}^\prime} k_\rho(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}'),\) (11)

where _u<sub>h</sub>_ is the kernel approximation to the unknown solution, **z** is an arbitrary evaluation point, \(\alpha_j\) is the coefficient associated with the _j_th constraint, and \(\mathbf{z}'\) is the second argument of the kernel. The superscript on \(\ell_j^{\mathbf{z}^\prime}\) indicates that the _j_th constraint functional acts on the second kernel argument, including evaluation at the location associated with that constraint. When the functional contains derivatives, these are applied before evaluating at the corresponding constraint location.

The representer formulation follows from the connection between finite-feature models and their continuum-kernel counterparts, as detailed in Appendix A.

Applying each constraint functional \(\ell_i\) to eq. 11 produces the linear system associated with the discrete PDE and physical conditions. Its coefficient matrix is the operator Gram matrix \(K_{\ell\ell}\), with entries

\((K_{\ell\ell})_{ij}=\ell_i^\mathbf{z}\ell_j^{\mathbf{z}^\prime} k_\rho(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}'),i,j=1,\dots,N,\) (12)

where \(\ell_i^\mathbf{z}\) and \(\ell_j^{\mathbf{z}^\prime}\) act on the first and second kernel arguments, respectively. Both functionals include evaluation at their prescribed constraint locations. Thus, \((K_{\ell\ell})_{ij}\) represents the interaction between the _i_th and _j_th constraint functionals through the continuum-feature mean kernel.

The matrix \(K_{\ell\ell}\) has dimensions \(N\times N\) and is symmetric and positive semidefinite. As established in eq. 8, its entries are the analytical population limits of the corresponding finite-feature constraint Gram-matrix entries.

Let \(\alpha=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_N)^\top\) denote the vector of representer coefficients and \(\mathbf{y}=(y_1,\dots,y_N)^\top\) the vector of prescribed constraint values. A regularized collocation formulation is then given by

\((K_{\ell\ell}+\lambda I)\alpha=\mathbf{y},\) (13)

where _I_ is the \(N\times N\) identity matrix and \(\lambda\ge 0\) is a prescribed regularization parameter. When \(\lambda=0\), the system corresponds to direct constraint interpolation, provided a solution exists. A positive regularization parameter improves the conditioning of the coefficient system but generally relaxes exact satisfaction of the discrete constraints. The separate enforcement of linear physical conditions through a null-space parameterization is described in the subsequent formulation.

Once the coefficient vector \(\alpha\) has been determined, the approximate solution can be evaluated at any point **z** using

\(u_h(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{z}\ell}^\top\alpha,(\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{z}\ell})_j=\ell_j^{\mathbf{z}^\prime} k_\rho(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}'),\) (14)

where \(\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{z}\ell}\) is an _N_-component column vector containing the kernel interactions between the evaluation point **z** and the selected constraint functionals. Its _j_th component is obtained by applying the _j_th functional to the second argument of the continuum-feature mean kernel. The superscript \(\top\) denotes vector transposition.

Equations 7-14 define the kernel formulation without retaining the finite number of Gaussian RBF features or their individual center realizations. Because the bounded continuum-feature mean kernel is evaluated analytically, no numerical quadrature over the feature-center distribution is required. The resulting PDE approximation is determined by the prescribed kernel parameters, the selected constraint locations, and the numerical treatment of the resulting collocation system.

## 2.3 Constraint-compatible enforcement of physical conditions

When boundary or initial data are to be satisfied independently of the PDE least-squares fit, we separate the physical constraints from the interior PDE equations. Let

\(A\alpha\approx\mathbf{f},B\alpha=\mathbf{g},\) (15)

denote, respectively, the interior PDE equations and the boundary or initial constraints obtained from the CFKS representation eq. 11.

A particular coefficient vector satisfying the physical constraints is chosen as

\(\alpha_p=B^+\mathbf{g},\) (16)

where _B_<sup>+</sup> denotes the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse. Let the columns of _Q_ span the numerical null space of _B_,

\(BQ=0.\) (17)

Every constraint-compatible solution can then be parameterized as

\(\alpha=\alpha_p+Q\eta.\) (18)

Substitution into the PDE equations gives the reduced problem

\(AQ\eta\approx\mathbf{f}-A\alpha_p.\) (19)

With Tikhonov regularization,

\(\eta=argmin_\eta\|AQ\eta-(\mathbf{f}-A\alpha_p)\|_2^2+\lambda\|\eta\|_2^2.\) (20)

This construction separates satisfaction of the linear physical constraints from fitting of the PDE residual and avoids introducing an arbitrary relative penalty between boundary and interior equations. In practice, the reduced system is solved using rank-revealing SVD-based linear algebra.

## 2.4 Nonlinear CFKS formulation

We now extend the continuum-feature kernel formulation to nonlinear differential problems. Consider

\(\mathcal{N}[u](\mathbf{z})=f(\mathbf{z}),\mathbf{z}\in\Omega,\) (21)

where N is a prescribed nonlinear differential operator, _u_ is the unknown solution, _f_ is a known source function, and \(\Omega\) is the computational domain. The operator may depend nonlinearly on the solution, its derivatives, or both. Appropriate boundary and, when applicable, initial conditions complete the problem.

Unlike the linear formulation, a nonlinear differential operator does not generally produce a fixed operator Gram matrix. Instead, CFKS constructs a deterministic kernel trial representation and determines its coefficients by minimizing the nonlinear PDE residual.

Let \(k_\rho\) be the continuum-feature mean kernel defined in eq. 7. We consider the trial representation

\(u_h(\mathbf{z};\unknown)=u_\mathrm{base}(\mathbf{z})+w(\mathbf{z})\sum_{j=1}^{N_r}\alpha_jk_\rho(\mathbf{z},\unknown_j),\) (22)

where _u<sub>h</sub>_ denotes the approximate solution, \(\unknown=(\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_{N_r})^\top\) is the unknown coefficient vector, _N<sub>r</sub>_ is the number of kernel representer sites, and \(\unknown_j\) is the location of the _j_th representer site. The prescribed functions _u_<sub>base</sub> and _w_ define an additive component and a multiplicative factor, respectively.

When a suitable analytical constraint embedding is available, these functions can be selected so that the trial solution satisfies the prescribed boundary or initial conditions independently of the coefficient values. An unconstrained representation is recovered by setting _u_<sub>base</sub>=0 and _w_=1.

The trial representation is linear in \(\unknown\), although the governing PDE residual is generally nonlinear in these coefficients. Importantly, _N<sub>r</sub>_ determines the dimension of the discrete kernel representation and does not represent the number of Gaussian RBF features. Each kernel section is already obtained by analytically averaging a continuum of Gaussian RBF features over the prescribed center distribution.

Let \(\{\mathbf{z}_i\}_{i=1}^{N_p}\) denote the interior PDE collocation locations, where _N<sub>p</sub>_ is the number of discrete PDE constraints. The residual at the _i_th collocation point is defined as

\(r_i(\unknown)=\mathcal{N}\left[u_h(\cdot;\unknown)\right](\mathbf{z}_i)-f(\mathbf{z}_i),i=1,\dots,N_p,\) (23)

where the nonlinear operator acts on the trial solution before evaluation at **z**_<sub>i</sub>_.

Collecting the residuals into the vector \(\mathbf{r}(\unknown)=(r_1,\dots,r_{N_p})^\top\), the kernel coefficients are determined through

\(\unknown^*=\mathrm{arg}\mathrm{min}_\unknown\frac{1}{2}\left\|\mathbf{r}(\unknown)\right\|_2^2,\) (24)

where \(\unknown^*\) denotes the optimized coefficient vector and \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is the Euclidean norm. Thus, the nonlinear PDE is enforced through least-squares minimization of its discrete residual.

The analytical continuum-feature kernel also permits direct construction of the residual Jacobian. Define the coefficient- independent trial functions

\(\psi_j(\mathbf{z})=w(\mathbf{z})k_\rho(\mathbf{z},\unknown_j),j=1,\dots,N_r.\) (25)

Since the derivative of the trial solution with respect to \(\alpha_j\) is \(\psi_j\), the Jacobian entries are

\(J_{ij}(\unknown)=\frac{\partial r_i}{\partial\alpha_j}=(\mathcal{N}'[u_h]\psi_j)(\mathbf{z}_i),\) (26)

provided the nonlinear operator is Fréchet differentiable. Here, \(\mathcal{N}'[u_h]\) denotes the linearization of N about the current trial solution, acting on the function \(\psi_j\). The Jacobian \(J(\unknown)\) has dimensions \(N_p\times N_r\).

Because the mean kernel and its derivatives are available analytically, the residual and Jacobian can be evaluated without generating finite random-feature realizations. The nonlinear optimization therefore determines only the coefficients of the prescribed continuum-feature kernel representation.

## Linearized initialization

The nonlinear least-squares problem generally requires an initial coefficient vector. A suitable initialization can be obtained by linearizing the governing equation about an available approximation.

Let _u_<sup>(_k_)</sup> denote the current approximation at iteration _k_, and let \(\delta u\) be a correction. A first-order expansion gives

\(\mathcal{N}[u^{(k)}+\delta u]\approx\mathcal{N}[u^{(k)}]+\mathcal{N}'[u^{(k)}]\delta u,\) (27)

where \(\mathcal{N}'[u^{(k)}]\) is the Fréchet derivative of the nonlinear operator evaluated at _u_<sup>(_k_)</sup>. The corresponding linearized equation is

\(\mathcal{N}'[u^{(k)}]\delta u\approx f-\mathcal{N}[u^{(k)}].\) (28)

For a fixed approximation _u_<sup>(_k_)</sup>, this is a linear differential problem for the correction \(\delta u\). Its discretization can use the analytical kernel derivatives developed for linear CFKS.

Alternatively, a Picard-type approximation may be used when the nonlinear operator admits an appropriate coefficient- freezing formulation. The resulting linearized solution supplies initial coefficients for the nonlinear least-squares problem eq. 24.

This initialization procedure does not replace the nonlinear coefficient solve. Rather, it provides a starting approximation for minimizing the full nonlinear PDE residual.

## Multiscale continuum-feature kernels

For problems with localized gradients or multiple characteristic scales, the trial representation can combine continuum-feature mean kernels with different prescribed Gaussian widths and center distributions.

We consider an additive global-local kernel of the form

\(k_\mathrm{ms}^{(s)}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}')=\widehat{k}_g^{(s)}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}')+\eta\widehat{k}_\ell^{(s)}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}'),\eta>0,\) (29)

where \(k_\mathrm{ms}^{(s)}\) is the multiscale kernel at refinement stage _s_, and \(\eta\) is a prescribed positive mixing weight. The subscripts _g_ and \(\ell\) identify the global and local components, respectively.

The global kernel is constructed from a bounded distribution of Gaussian centers covering the spatial domain, whereas the local kernel uses a center distribution concentrated around a prescribed region of interest. Each component is an analytically marginalized Gaussian-RBF mean kernel of the form defined in eq. 7.

To balance their contributions, the components are normalized according to

\(\widehat{k}_q^{(s)}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}')=\frac{k_q^{(s)}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}')}{k_q^{(s)}(\mathbf{z}_\mathrm{ref},\mathbf{z}_\mathrm{ref})},q\in\{g,\ell\},\) (30)

where _q_ identifies the kernel component and **z**<sub>ref</sub> is a prescribed reference point at which the diagonal kernel value is positive.

Positive normalization factors preserve positive semidefiniteness, and the positive weighted sum in eq. 29 remains a symmetric positive-semidefinite kernel. Its derivatives are obtained by differentiating the analytical component kernels.

The center distributions, Gaussian widths, normalization point, and mixing weight remain prescribed parameters. The multiscale construction therefore increases representation flexibility without introducing finite Gaussian-feature center sampling.

## Illustration using viscous Burgers’ equation

As a nonlinear example, consider the one-dimensional viscous Burgers equation

\(u_t+uu_x-\nu u_{xx}=0,(x,t)\in[-1,1]\times(0,T],\) (31)

where _x_ denotes the spatial coordinate, _t_ is time, _T_ is the final simulation time, and \(\nu>0\) is the viscosity. The subscripts _t_, _x_, and _xx_ denote the corresponding first time, first spatial, and second spatial derivatives.

For the homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions and prescribed initial profile used in this benchmark, analytical constraint embedding is applied on successive space-time slabs.

Let _n_ index the time slabs, with \(\tau=t-t_n\) denoting the local time measured from the beginning _t<sub>n</sub>_ of the current slab. At refinement stage _s_, the trial solution is

\(u_{h,n}^{(s)}(x,\tau)=u_{\mathrm{in},n}^{(s)}(x)+\tau(1-x^2)v_{h,n}^{(s)}(x,\tau),\) (32)

where \(u_{\mathrm{in},n}^{(s)}\) is the incoming solution profile and \(v_{h,n}^{(s)}\) is an unknown correction field.

The factors \(\tau\) and 1-_x_<sup>2</sup> make the correction vanish at the beginning of each slab and at the spatial boundaries, respectively. Hence, the trial solution preserves the incoming profile and satisfies the homogeneous boundary conditions, provided the incoming profile is boundary-compatible.

The correction field is represented by

\(v_{h,n}^{(s)}(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{j=1}^{N_{p,n}^{(s)}}\alpha_{j,n}^{(s)}k_\mathrm{ms}^{(s)}(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}_{j,n}^{(s)}),\) (33)

where \(\mathbf{z}=(x,\tau)\), \(N_{p,n}^{(s)}\) is the number of PDE collocation points on slab _n_ at stage _s_, \(\mathbf{z}_{j,n}^{(s)}\) denotes the corresponding collocation location, and \(\alpha_{j,n}^{(s)}\) is its kernel coefficient. Thus, the PDE collocation locations also serve as kernel represententer sites. For a fixed slab and stage, let \(\unknown\) collect the unknown coefficients, with the slab and stage indices suppressed for simplicity. Analytical differentiation of the embedded trial solution gives the affine relations \(\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}_\mathrm{in}+D_u\unknown,\)
\(\mathbf{u}_x=\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{in},x}+D_{u_x}\unknown,\)
\(\mathbf{u}_{xx}=\mathbf{u}_{\mathrm{in},xx}+D_{u_{xx}}\unknown,\)
\(\mathbf{u}_t=D_{u_t}\unknown,\) (34) where the vectors on the left contain the solution and its derivatives at the PDE collocation points. The vectors **u**in, **u**in_,x_, and **u**in_,xx_ contain the incoming profile and its spatial derivatives at those points. The matrices _Du_, _Dux_, _Duxx_, and _Dut_ represent the corresponding contributions of the kernel correction, including derivatives of the analytical embedding factor. The incoming profile has no local-time dependence and therefore contributes nothing to the time derivative. The discrete nonlinear residual is \(\mathbf{r}(\unknown)=\mathbf{u}_t+\mathbf{u}\odot\mathbf{u}_x-\nu\mathbf{u}_{xx},\) (35) where \(\odot\) denotes componentwise multiplication. Differentiating this residual with respect to the kernel coefficients yields \(J(\unknown)=D_{u_t}+\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{u}_x)D_u+\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{u})D_{u_x}-\nu D_{u_{xx}},\) (36) where \(\mathrm{diag}(\cdot)\) denotes the diagonal matrix formed from a vector. The nonlinear coefficients are obtained by minimizing the residual in eq. 35 using the analytical Jacobian in eq. 36. Linearized initialization, multiscale kernel refinement, and residual-guided collocation are used in the numerical implementation, with the specific settings described in the benchmark setup. ## 2.5 Residual-adaptive collocation The continuum-feature kernel formulation permits either fixed or adaptive PDE collocation. A fixed deterministic point distribution is sufficient when it adequately resolves the solution. For problems with localized under-resolution, residual-adaptive collocation can concentrate additional PDE constraints in regions where the current approximation exhibits larger governing-equation residuals. This refinement mechanism is not required by CFKS itself. It provides an additional resolution strategy that can be combined with linear or nonlinear kernel formulations. To describe both cases, define the PDE residual operator \(\mathcal{R}[u]=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c } \mathcal{L}u-f, & \text{for a linear PDE}, \\ \mathcal{N}[u]-f, & \text{for a nonlinear PDE}, \end{array}\right.\) (37) where L and N are the prescribed linear and nonlinear differential operators, respectively, and _f_ is the corresponding source function. Let P(0) denote an initial deterministic PDE collocation set, and let _u_(0) be the CFKS approximation obtained from this set. We refer to _u_(0) as the predictor solution. The computational region is partitioned into _NB_ blocks, denoted by \(\{\Omega_b\}_{b=1}^{N_B}\), where _b_ is the block index. For each block, define an independent residual probe set \(\mathcal{Q}_b\subset\Omega_b\). The probe points are distinct from the PDE collocation locations used to construct the predictor. At a probe point **q**, the predictor residual is \(r^{(0)}(\mathbf{q})=\mathcal{R}[u^{(0)}](\mathbf{q}),\) (38) where _r_(0) measures the discrepancy between the governing differential equation and the predictor approximation. The residual magnitude within each block is characterized by its root-mean-square and maximum values, \(R_b^\mathrm{rms}=\left(\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}_b|}\sum_{\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{Q}_b}|r^{(0)}(\mathbf{q})|^2\right)^{1/2},R_b^\mathrm{max}=\mathrm{max}_{\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{Q}_b}|r^{(0)}(\mathbf{q})|.\) (39)

Here, |Q_<sub>b</sub>_| is the number of probe points in block _b_, \(R_b^\mathrm{rms}\) measures the average residual magnitude, and \(R_b^\mathrm{max}\) measures the largest observed residual.

A normalized residual indicator is constructed by combining these measures:

\(s_b=\omega\frac{R_b^\mathrm{rms}}{\mathrm{max}_{1\le j\le N_B}R_j^\mathrm{rms}+\varepsilon}+(1-\omega)\frac{R_b^\mathrm{max}}{\mathrm{max}_{1\le j\le N_B}R_j^\mathrm{max}+\varepsilon},\) (40)

where _s<sub>b</sub>_ is the indicator for block _b_, \(\omega\in[0,1]\) is a prescribed weighting parameter, and \(\varepsilon>0\) prevents division by zero. The index _j_ runs over all blocks in the region being refined. The two terms measure, respectively, the relative average residual and the relative peak residual.

The indicator determines the refinement level assigned to each block. For a three-level strategy, define

\(\gamma_b=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\mathrm{high}, & s_b\ge s_\mathrm{high}, \\
\mathrm{mid}, & s_\mathrm{mid}\le s_b<s_\mathrm{high}, \\
\mathrm{low}, & s_b<s_\mathrm{mid},
\end{array}\right.\) (41)

where \(\gamma_b\) denotes the refinement level, and _s_<sub>mid</sub> and _s_<sub>high</sub> are prescribed thresholds satisfying \(0\le s_\mathrm{mid}<s_\mathrm{high}\).

The levels correspond to prescribed collocation budgets _N_<sub>low</sub>, _N_<sub>mid</sub>, and _N_<sub>high</sub>. The number of PDE collocation points assigned to block _b_, denoted by _N<sub>b</sub>_, is selected according to its refinement level \(\gamma_b\). The total number of PDE collocation points after refinement is therefore

\(N_p^\mathrm{ref}=\sum_{b=1}^{N_B}N_b,\) (42)

where \(N_p^\mathrm{ref}\) is the total refined collocation budget.

Additional implementation rules may be introduced to avoid abrupt spatial changes in collocation density, such as extending high-refinement assignments to neighboring blocks. The particular thresholds, point budgets, and neighboring- block rules are selected for the numerical problem under study.

Once the blockwise budgets are determined, the refined PDE collocation locations are generated within the corresponding blocks. Deterministic low-discrepancy sequences provide one means of constructing these point sets without introducing random sampling.

For a prescribed continuum-feature mean kernel, residual-guided collocation refinement modifies the discrete PDE constraints but does not change the analytical kernel itself. If the kernel representer sites coincide with the collocation locations, as in the nonlinear implementation considered here, enrichment also changes the number of kernel coefficients.

Residual-guided collocation may additionally be combined with prescribed changes in Gaussian kernel widths or center distributions. In that case, the discrete collocation representation and the underlying kernel parameters are both modified.

In the viscous Burgers experiment, residual-adaptive collocation forms part of the second stage of a predictor-corrector procedure. Residual indicators computed from the completed predictor determine the corrector collocation distribution. The corrector also employs narrower prescribed kernel widths, so the resulting accuracy improvement cannot be attributed to collocation adaptation alone.

The numerical values used for the residual weights, refinement thresholds, probe distributions, and collocation budgets are specified with the corresponding test problem.

## Residual-adaptive collocation settings

The two-stage Burgers computation uses a deterministic predictor followed by a residual-guided corrector. The spatial interval is divided into 20 equal blocks. For each time slab, the predictor uses 10 PDE collocation points per block, giving 200 points per slab.

The predictor residual is evaluated independently on a tensor-product probe grid within each block, using 11 spatial locations and 7 local-time locations. Spatial probe positions extend from 5% to 95% of the block width, while the local-time positions range from \(0.08\Delta t\) to \(0.96\Delta t\), where \(\Delta t\) is the slab duration. Thus, each block contains 77 residual probes.

The residual indicator in eq. 40 uses \(\omega=0.7\), assigning weights of 0.7 and 0.3 to the root-mean-square and maximum residual measures, respectively. The refinement thresholds in eq. 41 are prescribed as _s_<sub>mid</sub>=0.10 and _s_<sub>high</sub>=0.35.

To reduce abrupt changes in collocation density, high- and medium-refinement assignments are extended to immediately adjacent spatial blocks. The expansion does not wrap around the domain boundaries, and high-refinement assignments take precedence where the expanded regions overlap.

The corrector uses the blockwise collocation budgets

\(N_\mathrm{low}=10,N_\mathrm{mid}=20,N_\mathrm{high}=30.\) (43)

The residual normalization and refinement decisions are performed separately for each time slab. Consequently, the corrector collocation count varies with the residual distribution.

Collocation points in both stages are generated using a deterministic two-dimensional Halton sequence with bases 2 and 3. Within each spatial block, the first _N<sub>b</sub>_ Halton points are mapped to the corresponding spatial and local-time intervals, where _N<sub>b</sub>_ is the prescribed blockwise point budget.

The Stage 2 corrector combines this residual-guided collocation enrichment with narrower prescribed global and local Gaussian kernel widths. The kernel representer sites coincide with the PDE collocation locations in both stages.

## 2.6 Sequential space-time-slab formulation

For time-dependent PDEs, CFKS can be applied sequentially over consecutive space-time slabs rather than constructing a single kernel approximation over the entire temporal domain. This strategy reduces the size of the individual space-time problems and allows the solution to be advanced through a sequence of local temporal intervals.

Let \(\Omega_x\) denote the spatial domain and [_t_<sub>0</sub>_,T_] the temporal interval, where _t_<sub>0</sub> is the initial time and _T_ is the final time. The temporal interval is partitioned into _N<sub>T</sub>_ consecutive slabs,

\(I_n=[t_n,t_{n+1}],n=0,\dots,N_T-1,\) (44)

where _n_ is the slab index, _N<sub>T</sub>_ denotes the total number of slabs, and the partition points satisfy

\(t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_{N_T}=T.\) (45)

The duration of slab _n_ is \(\Delta t_n=t_{n+1}-t_n>0\).

Within each slab, the physical time coordinate is replaced by the local coordinate

\(\tau=t-t_n,0\le\tau\le\Delta t_n,\) (46)

where \(\tau=0\) and \(\tau=\Delta t_n\) correspond to the beginning and end of the current slab, respectively.

The CFKS approximation on slab _n_ is denoted by \(u_n(\mathbf{x},\tau)\), where **x** represents the spatial coordinates. The governing PDE is enforced at selected collocation points within the corresponding space-time region \(\Omega_x\times(0,\Delta t_n]\). The same continuum-feature kernel formulation developed in the preceding sections applies to each slab.

The local coordinate system permits the same analytical mean-kernel construction to be used across different slabs. When the slab durations, local collocation configurations, and prescribed kernel parameters are identical, the corresponding kernel matrices and analytical derivative evaluations may also be reused.

### Sequential transfer of the solution

The initial condition for each slab is obtained from the prescribed initial data or from the terminal solution of the preceding slab.

Let _u_<sub>init</sub>(**x**) denote the prescribed initial profile at time _t_<sub>0</sub>. The sequential transfer condition is

\(u_n(\mathbf{x},0)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
u_\mathrm{init}(\mathbf{x}), & n=0, \\
u_{n-1}(\mathbf{x},\Delta t_{n-1}), & n>0,
\end{array}\right.\) (47)

where \(u_{n-1}(\mathbf{x},\Delta t_{n-1})\) represents the terminal profile of the preceding slab.

Thus, each local space-time problem receives its initial data from the preceding time interval. The solution is advanced sequentially until the final time is reached.

The incoming profile may be imposed through discrete initial constraints or incorporated analytically into a constraint- compatible trial representation. In either case, the local approximation is constructed to match the prescribed incoming data according to the chosen constraint-enforcement procedure.

In numerical implementations, the terminal profile may be transferred directly or represented through an interpolation procedure. When interpolation is used, the incoming profile is an approximation of the preceding terminal solution, and the transfer accuracy becomes part of the overall temporal discretization error.

Within each slab, the CFKS representation remains global over the spatial domain. The temporal decomposition therefore does not introduce artificial spatial interfaces or require spatial domain decomposition.

### Predictor-corrector slab marching

Sequential slab marching can also be combined with residual-adaptive collocation. In this case, a predictor solution is first computed using an initial deterministic collocation distribution.

Let \(u_n^{(0)}(\mathbf{x},\tau)\) denote the predictor approximation on slab _n_, where the superscript (0) identifies the predictor stage. The predictor satisfies the sequential transfer condition

\(u_n^{(0)}(\mathbf{x},0)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
u_\mathrm{init}(\mathbf{x}), & n=0, \\
u_{n-1}^{(0)}(\mathbf{x},\Delta t_{n-1}), & n>0.
\end{array}\right.\) (48)

The predictor is advanced through the entire temporal interval, with each slab initialized from the preceding predictor slab.

After completing the predictor march, the PDE residual is evaluated at independent probe locations, as described in Section 2.5. The resulting residual indicators identify regions requiring additional collocation resolution.

Let \(\gamma_{b,n}\) denote the refinement level assigned to block _b_ on slab _n_, where _b_ is the spatial-block index. These refinement assignments determine the collocation distribution used for the subsequent corrector computation.

The corrector solution, denoted by \(u_n^{(1)}(\mathbf{x},\tau)\), is then computed through a second sequential march, with

\(u_n^{(1)}(\mathbf{x},0)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
u_\mathrm{init}(\mathbf{x}), & n=0, \\
u_{n-1}^{(1)}(\mathbf{x},\Delta t_{n-1}), & n>0.
\end{array}\right.\) (49)

where the superscript (1) identifies the corrector stage.

The predictor and corrector marches are performed independently, each beginning from the prescribed initial condition. The predictor residual information determines the refined collocation distributions, but the predictor solution is not imposed as the initial profile of the corrector.

Instead, continuity between successive corrector slabs is maintained through the terminal profile of the preceding corrector slab, subject to the selected numerical transfer procedure.

The corrector may retain the prescribed mean kernel used by the predictor or employ different prescribed kernel parameters. In the latter case, residual-guided collocation refinement and kernel-scale refinement are combined within the same sequential solution strategy.

### General characteristics

Sequential space-time-slab marching is compatible with both linear and nonlinear CFKS formulations. The governing PDE is discretized independently within each slab, while the incoming solution profile supplies the initial data required for temporal advancement.

For linear problems, the local coefficients can be determined through the corresponding kernel collocation or constraint- compatible linear least-squares formulation. For nonlinear problems, the same slab decomposition can be combined with linearized initialization and nonlinear residual minimization.

The continuum-feature mean kernel and its analytical differential operators remain applicable within every slab. Temporal decomposition changes the organization of the discrete PDE solve without reintroducing finite Gaussian RBF feature realizations.

Residual-guided predictor-corrector marching is an additional refinement strategy rather than a requirement of the sequential formulation.

## 4.3 Poisson and biharmonic problems on the five-petal domain

Figure 2 summarizes the CFKS results for the Poisson and biharmonic problems on the irregular five-petal domain. The top row corresponds to the second-order Poisson problem and the bottom row to the fourth-order biharmonic problem.

For the Poisson case, CFKS reproduces the manufactured solution over the entire nonconvex domain with an independent solution RMSE of \(4.32\times 10^{-4}\) and a maximum absolute error of \(2.37\times 10^{-3}\). The maximum boundary error is \(2.23\times 10^{-5}\), confirming that the Dirichlet constraint is maintained accurately by the null-space formulation. The independent PDE residual has RMS \(7.32\times 10^{-1}\) and maximum magnitude 8.79. As seen in the top row of Fig. 2, the largest solution errors remain localized within the interior rather than being distributed uniformly over the domain.

The biharmonic problem provides a more demanding test because it requires fourth-order population-kernel derivatives together with simultaneous Dirichlet and normal-derivative boundary conditions. CFKS achieves an independent solution RMSE of \(1.71\times 10^{-3}\) and a maximum absolute error of \(6.51\times 10^{-3}\). The maximum training boundary error is \(1.21\times 10^{-5}\), while the dense Dirichlet-boundary error is \(1.05\times 10^{-6}\). The biharmonic residual has RMS \(2.83\times 10^3\) and maximum magnitude \(3.09\times 10^4\). Although the absolute residual is larger than in the Poisson case, this reflects the substantially larger scale introduced by repeated differentiation in the fourth-order operator; the solution itself remains accurate throughout the domain. The total CFKS solve time is 0.736 s, comprising approximately 0.663 s for kernel/operator assembly, 0.046 s for the null-space construction, and 0.020 s for the reduced SVD solve. The dominant computational cost is therefore the assembly of the high-order operator-kernel matrices rather than the constrained linear solve.

The two cases therefore show that the same CFKS construction extends from second- to fourth-order operators on irregular geometries without altering the underlying population-kernel representation. They also demonstrate that the center-support geometry need not coincide with the physical domain: the nonconvex boundary enters through the physical constraint functionals, while the population kernel is defined on the surrounding embedding region.

## 4.4 Singularly perturbed problem

Figure 3 illustrates the predictor-residual-corrector behavior for the singularly perturbed boundary-value problem with \(\nu=10^{-3}\). The coarse predictor captures the outer solution but under-resolves the narrow boundary layer near _x_=1. This is reflected by the independent residual indicator, which remains negligible over most of the interval and rises sharply only in the boundary-layer region. As a result, the adaptive strategy assigns 97 blocks to the low level, one to the mid level, and only two to the high level.

The predictor uses 200 PDE collocation points and yields an RMSE of \(5.95\times 10^{-3}\) with a maximum error of \(1.82\times 10^{-1}\). After residual-guided enrichment, the corrector uses 250 PDE points and reduces the RMSE to \(1.76\times 10^{-3}\) and the maximum error to \(6.50\times 10^{-2}\). Thus, the adaptive corrector improves the RMSE by a factor of 3.38 and the maximum error by a factor of 2.80 relative to a budget-matched uniform discretization using the same 250 PDE points. The uniform reference remains essentially unchanged from the coarse predictor, with an RMSE of \(5.95\times 10^{-3}\), showing that the improvement is due to where the additional constraints are placed rather than simply to their number.

The adaptive set uses only 10.42% of the fully enriched budget obtained by assigning 24 PDE points to every block. The predictor kernel assembly and spectral solve require approximately 0.047 and 0.030 s, respectively, while residual probing and level assignment require about 0.191 s in the recorded run. The adaptive corrector requires approximately 0.090 s for kernel assembly and 0.034 s for the spectral solve, giving a total CFKS corrector solve time of 0.123 s. These results show that the residual-adaptive stage concentrates additional constraints in the boundary-layer region while leaving the underlying CFKS representation unchanged.

For context, the same singularly perturbed steady advection-diffusion problem with \(\nu=10^{-3}\) was considered by De Florio et al. \[24\]. Their experiments used _N_<sub>int</sub>=10<sup>4</sup> interior collocation points for all methods, while the accurate ELM-based PIELM and X-TFC configurations also employed 10<sup>4</sup> hidden neurons at this parameter value. In contrast, the present CFKS predictor uses only 200 PDE collocation points, and the residual-adaptive corrector increases this number to 250 by concentrating additional points near the localized boundary layer. Thus, rather than increasing the global representation and collocation budgets, CFKS exploits the independently evaluated residual to allocate resolution only where it is needed.

## 4.5 Advection and advection-diffusion

We first consider two time-dependent transport problems to examine the performance of sequential space-time-slab marching and residual-adaptive collocation. The governing equations, computational domains, and reference solutions are summarized in  1. Both experiments employ a deterministic coarse predictor followed by a residual-guided corrector, with the continuum-feature mean kernel retained between the two stages. Independent residual evaluations are used to identify regions of under-resolution and redistribute the PDE collocation points accordingly. Figures 4 and 5 illustrate the resulting predictor and corrector solutions, residual distributions, and space-time collocation patterns.

For the linear advection problem, a narrow Gaussian pulse propagates periodically across the spatial domain \[-1,1\] with unit advection speed. The coarse predictor captures the overall motion of the pulse but accumulates visible phase and amplitude errors during propagation. At the final time _t_=1, the predictor has a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of \(6.53\times 10^{-2}\) and a maximum absolute error of \(3.73\times 10^{-1}\). The independently evaluated residual identifies a narrow moving region of under-resolution, producing a high-attention space-time band aligned with the pulse trajectory, as shown in Fig. 4. Residual-guided collocation enrichment follows this band and reduces the final RMSE to \(2.87\times 10^{-3}\) and the maximum absolute error to \(2.13\times 10^{-2}\). The corrector uses an average of 307.0 PDE collocation points per slab, with a minimum of 288 and a maximum of 320 points. The improved agreement with the exact solution demonstrates that localized enrichment can resolve the transported feature without changing the prescribed continuum-feature kernel.

The computational timings distinguish the cost of the kernel solution from the additional operations required for residual diagnostics and sequential transfer. For the advection predictor, kernel assembly, spectral factorization, and coefficient solution over all slabs require approximately 0.085, 0.119, and 0.054 s, respectively, giving a core CFKS time of 0.259 s. Residual probing and slab prediction/transfer require approximately 19.48 and 12.70 s, respectively, and therefore dominate the predictor-stage computational cost. For the adaptive corrector, the core CFKS time increases to 4.64 s, including 0.103 s for full operator-kernel assembly and 4.30 s for cached spectral factorizations associated with 52 distinct refinement patterns. The total Stage-2 elapsed time, including prediction and transfer, is 20.16 s. These measurements indicate that the cost of independent residual evaluation and dense solution transfer can substantially exceed that of the underlying population-kernel coefficient solve.

In the pure advection case, the enrichment follows the narrow trajectory of the periodically transported pulse, whereas in the advection-diffusion case it adapts to a translating and broadening profile. The accuracy improvements are obtained by changing the locations and number of discrete PDE constraints rather than introducing additional finite Gaussian-RBF features or sampling new feature centers. This distinction is important because the adaptive procedure operates on the discretization of the governing equations while the analytically prescribed mean kernel remains unchanged. The results also indicate that improving the efficiency of residual probing and slab-to-slab transfer is a relevant direction for reducing the overall computational cost of time-dependent CFKS implementations.

Closely related sharp-gradient transport benchmarks were previously used to motivate the distributed physics-informed extreme learning machine (PIELM) formulation \[21\], in which spatial domain decomposition was introduced to improve the resolution of localized solution structures. In contrast, the present CFKS computations retain a spatially global continuum-feature kernel representation within each time slab, without introducing artificial spatial interface conditions. Localized structures are instead resolved by redistributing PDE collocation points according to independently evaluated residual information. The resulting calculations illustrate how deterministic population-kernel representations can be combined with adaptive collocation without requiring spatial domain decomposition.

## 4.6 Viscous Burgers equation

We next consider the nonlinear viscous Burgers equation to examine the applicability of CFKS beyond linear differential operators. The problem is solved directly at viscosity \(\nu=0.01\) over \([-1,1]\times[0,1]\), with initial condition \(u(x,0)=-sin(\pi x)\) and homogeneous Dirichlet conditions at both spatial boundaries. The numerical solution is compared with a Cole-Hopf reference solution. At this viscosity, nonlinear steepening produces a sharp internal transition near _x_=0, providing a demanding test of the continuum-feature representation, analytical kernel derivatives, and nonlinear residual minimization. The calculation employs a two-stage predictor-corrector strategy combining prescribed multiscale kernel refinement with residual-guided collocation enrichment. Unlike the linear transport experiments, both the collocation distribution and the Gaussian kernel widths are modified between the two stages.

The temporal interval is divided into 40 uniform space-time slabs, each of duration \(\Delta t=0.025\), while the spatial interval is partitioned into 20 equal blocks for residual assessment and collocation refinement. On each slab, the analytical trial-function embedding in (32) preserves the incoming solution profile and homogeneous boundary conditions. After completing a slab, the terminal solution is evaluated on a uniform spatial transfer grid containing 1201 points, with the prescribed boundary values imposed at the endpoints. A cubic-spline interpolant of this terminal profile supplies the incoming solution and its spatial derivatives for the following slab. The predictor and corrector are marched separately through the complete temporal interval, each starting from the prescribed initial condition. The predictor residual information determines the corrector collocation distribution, but the predictor solution is not imposed as the incoming profile of the corrector.

The nonlinear approximation uses the normalized global-local continuum-feature mean kernel defined in (29), with prescribed mixing weight \(\eta=0.30\). The global Gaussian center distribution covers the spatial interval \[-1.3,1.3\], whereas the local component uses the narrower interval \[-0.3,0.3\] to provide additional resolution around the developing internal transition. The corresponding local-time center intervals are \([-0.04,\Delta t+0.04]\) for the global component and \([-0.035,\Delta t+0.035]\) for the local component. Each kernel component is normalized by its diagonal value at the spatial origin and the midpoint of the local time slab. For the Stage-1 predictor, the prescribed spatial and temporal Gaussian widths are (0.20,0.04) for the global kernel and (0.06,0.06) for the local kernel. In Stage 2, these widths are reduced to (0.10,0.02) and (0.015,0.015), respectively. The prescribed kernel parameters remain fixed across the slabs within each stage but differ between the predictor and corrector computations.

The nonlinear coefficient solution on each slab begins with a frozen-advection linearization based on the incoming solution profile, followed by a Picard update. The linearized coefficient systems are solved using singular-value- decomposition (SVD) regularization, with relative ridge factors of 10<sup>-8</sup> and 10<sup>-9</sup> for the frozen-advection and Picard steps, respectively. The resulting coefficients initialize nonlinear least-squares minimization of the full Burgers residual, using the analytical Jacobian derived in (36). ## 4.7 Finite-feature to continuum convergence

To verify the finite-feature interpretation of CFKS, we use the first-order oscillatory ODE benchmark defined in Sec. 3,

\(u'(x)=cos(15x),x\in[-2\pi,2\pi],u(0)=0,\) (50)

with exact solution \(u_\mathrm{ex}(x)=\frac{1}{15}sin(15x)\). This case provides a convenient controlled setting in which the finite Gaussian-RBF feature representation and the corresponding CFKS population limit can be compared directly.

Figure 8 verifies numerically that the finite Gaussian-RBF feature representation approaches the CFKS population limit as the number of sampled features _M_ increases. The top panel shows the relative Frobenius errors of the empirical value Gram matrix, \(\|K_M-K_\rho\|_F/\|K_\rho\|_F\), and of the operator-applied Gram matrix, \(\|G_M-G_\rho\|_F/\|G_\rho\|_F\). Both decrease systematically with _M_ and closely follow the reference _M_<sup>-1/2</sup> slope expected for Monte Carlo sampling of the center population. The mean value-kernel error decreases from 1.52 at _M_=25 to \(1.04\times 10^{-1}\) at _M_=5000, while the operator-Gram error decreases from 1.74 to \(1.18\times 10^{-1}\) over the same range. The shrinking realization-to-realization spread further confirms convergence toward a deterministic population kernel.

The bottom panel shows the corresponding effect at the solution level. For small feature counts, the finite-feature approximation remains far from the CFKS solution, with RMS differences of approximately \(6\times 10^{-2}\) for \(M\le 200\). A marked transition occurs once the feature space becomes sufficiently rich: at _M_=500 the mean finite-feature-to-CFKS RMSE falls to \(5.98\times 10^{-5}\), and subsequently decreases to \(4.45\times 10^{-6}\) at _M_=5000. The CFKS solution itself has an RMSE of \(1.54\times 10^{-5}\) relative to the exact solution. At large _M_, the finite-feature solutions therefore converge toward the deterministic CFKS reference, while their realization-dependent variability also decreases.

These results provide direct numerical evidence for the interpretation of CFKS as the population limit of the underlying finite Gaussian-RBF feature model. The continuum formulation removes the finite-feature sampling error and the associated realization variability, while retaining the operator Gram structure obtained from the original RBF representation.<tbc>

## 4.8 Conditioning and regularization

Figure 9 examines the sensitivity of CFKS to the two principal numerical parameters using the first-order oscillatory ODE benchmark. The regularization sweep shows the expected trade-off between stabilization and approximation accuracy: insufficient regularization leaves the solve sensitive to small singular values, whereas excessive regularization increases both the solution and residual errors. The baseline value \(\lambda_\mathrm{rel}=10^{-11}\) lies within the stable low-error region.

The lower panel shows that the Gaussian width \(\sigma\) has a strong effect on the conditioning of the reduced operator system. Increasing \(\sigma\) changes the overlap among neighboring population-kernel basis functions and can substantially increase the raw condition number. Tikhonov regularization reduces this effective conditioning burden while preserving the solution accuracy over a useful range of kernel widths. These results motivate the moderate width and weak regularization used throughout the remaining experiments.

## 4.10 Overall observations

The numerical experiments demonstrate the applicability of CFKS across differential problems involving oscillatory solutions, multiscale structures, irregular geometries, higher-order operators, localized boundary layers, time-dependent transport, and nonlinear dynamics. The finite-feature convergence study provides direct numerical evidence that empirical Gaussian-RBF value and operator Gram matrices approach their analytically defined continuum counterparts as the number of sampled features increases. This establishes the connection between finite Gaussian-RBF representations and the deterministic continuum-feature formulation used throughout the paper. The ODE, Poisson, and biharmonic benchmarks further demonstrate that the resulting mean kernel and its analytical derivatives can be employed for differential operators of different orders without introducing separate finite feature realizations. The successful treatment of the irregular five-petal domain also illustrates that the prescribed kernel center-support region need not coincide with the physical computational domain, since the domain geometry and physical conditions enter through the corresponding constraint functionals.

The singularly perturbed and time-dependent transport experiments demonstrate the role of residual-adaptive collocation as an additional resolution strategy within the continuum-feature framework. Independent PDE residual evaluations identify localized regions where the predictor approximation is insufficiently resolved, and the corrector redistributes collocation points accordingly. The singularly perturbed problem shows that concentrating additional constraints near a narrow boundary layer can be more effective than uniform refinement with the same point budget. Similarly, the advection and advection–diffusion experiments demonstrate that residual-guided enrichment can follow moving localized structures, while the two-pulse advection benchmark confirms that multiple separated regions of under-resolution can be identified simultaneously. In these linear examples, the prescribed continuum-feature mean kernel remains unchanged between the predictor and corrector stages; refinement modifies the discrete collocation representation rather than the underlying Gaussian feature distribution.

The viscous Burgers experiment extends the numerical assessment to a nonlinear differential operator. In this setting, the continuum-feature mean kernel defines a deterministic trial representation, while the unknown coefficients are determined through nonlinear least-squares residual minimization. Linearized initialization and analytical kernel derivatives provide the starting approximation, nonlinear residual, and corresponding Jacobian. At the investigated viscosity \(\nu=0.01\), the two-stage procedure substantially improves the resolution of the developing internal transition.<tbc>
