Unlike the linear transport experiments, however, the Burgers corrector combines residual-guided collocation enrichment with narrower prescribed Gaussian widths in a global-local multiscale kernel. The observed accuracy improvement therefore reflects their combined effect, and the present experiment does not separately quantify the contribution of either refinement mechanism.

The conditioning and timing results also clarify the computational characteristics of CFKS. The regularization and Gaussian-width study for the first-order ODE confirms that the accuracy and conditioning of the discrete operator-kernel system depend on these prescribed numerical parameters. In the steady linear benchmarks, the main computational costs are associated with analytical kernel assembly and dense linear algebra, while null-space construction contributes comparatively little to the measured solve times. For the slab-based transport problems, residual evaluation, dense solution prediction, and temporal transfer can require more computational time than the core kernel coefficient solves. Nonlinear problems introduce additional costs through repeated residual and Jacobian evaluations during iterative coefficient optimization. Consequently, the overall computational efficiency depends on both the kernel discretization and the numerical procedures used for refinement, diagnostics, and time advancement.

Taken together, these findings support CFKS as a deterministic computational framework connecting finite Gaussian- RBF feature representations with analytically constructed continuum-feature kernel PDE solvers. Its principal representational advantage is the elimination of the finite feature count and individual center-sampling variability, rather than the elimination of all numerical parameter choices. Gaussian widths, bounded center distributions, collocation configurations, regularization, and, where applicable, nonlinear initialization remain important aspects of the numerical formulation. The experiments demonstrate the flexibility of this approach across the considered benchmarks, while also identifying parameter selection, conditioning, and computational scalability as important considerations for broader applications.

**Remarks**

• **Scope of nonlinear validation.** The nonlinear CFKS formulation is demonstrated numerically using viscous Burgers’ equation at \(\nu=0.01\). Although the analytical kernel derivatives and nonlinear least-squares formulation are applicable to other sufficiently smooth nonlinear differential operators, their numerical accuracy, robustness, and convergence behavior have not been systematically investigated across broader classes of nonlinear PDEs. The reported Burgers corrector modifies both the collocation distribution and the prescribed multiscale kernel widths, so their individual effects cannot be distinguished from the present results. Further numerical studies involving different nonlinear operators, parameter regimes, and separate refinement strategies are needed to assess the generality and limitations of the nonlinear extension.<tbc>

• **Kernel parameters and numerical stability.** Although analytical marginalization removes finite-feature sampling variability, CFKS remains dependent on prescribed Gaussian widths, center distributions, and regularization parameters. The conditioning study illustrates the influence of Gaussian width and regularization on a representative linear problem, but does not establish a universally optimal parameter-selection rule. For problems containing localized structures, the appropriate kernel scales must also be considered in relation to the spatial and temporal resolution. In sequential space-time-slab computations, the accuracy of transferring the terminal solution between slabs provides an additional numerical consideration. Systematic parameter- selection procedures and conditioning-aware kernel refinement therefore remain worthwhile directions for further investigation.<tbc>

• **Computational scalability.** CFKS avoids explicit finite Gaussian-RBF feature realizations but retains the computational demands of dense kernel discretizations. For a linear system involving _N_ constraints, storing the full operator Gram matrix requires O(_N_<sup>2</sup>) memory, while direct dense factorization may require O(_N_<sup>3</sup>) operations. Nonlinear formulations additionally require repeated evaluation of the PDE residual and its Jacobian. Sequential space-time-slab marching limits the size of individual temporal problems, and residual- adaptive collocation can concentrate resolution in selected regions, but neither mechanism removes the general scalability limitations of dense kernel systems. Low-rank kernel approximations, matrix-free iterative methods, efficient residual evaluation, and localized or domain-decomposed formulations are potential approaches for extending CFKS to larger-scale applications.

## 5 Conclusions

This work introduced Continuum-Feature Kernel Solver (CFKS), a deterministic framework for solving differential equations through analytical marginalization of a bounded continuum of Gaussian radial basis function (RBF) features. By replacing a finite feature realization with its exact continuum-feature mean kernel, CFKS eliminates the need to prescribe a finite feature count or select individual feature centers. The resulting kernel and its differential-operator<tbc>

counterparts are evaluated analytically and used directly in the numerical discretization. For linear problems, this construction leads to symmetric operator-kernel collocation systems, with boundary and initial conditions enforced through constraint-compatible null-space parameterization. For nonlinear problems, the continuum-feature representation is retained, while the unknown coefficients are determined through linearized initialization and nonlinear least-squares residual minimization using analytical kernel derivatives and Jacobians.

The numerical investigations support the proposed formulation from both the feature-representation and differential- equation perspectives. Finite-feature convergence experiments demonstrate that empirical Gaussian-RBF value and operator Gram matrices approach their analytically derived continuum counterparts as the number of sampled features increases. The corresponding finite-feature solutions also approach the deterministic CFKS solution, confirming the computational connection between finite Gaussian-RBF models and the continuum-feature formulation. The linear benchmarks demonstrate the applicability of the analytical operator kernels to oscillatory and multiscale ODEs, second- and fourth-order elliptic problems on irregular domains, singularly perturbed boundary layers, and time-dependent transport equations. Residual-guided collocation enrichment further improves the resolution of localized solution structures without changing the underlying mean kernel in the linear adaptive examples. The transport experiments additionally demonstrate that this strategy can track multiple moving localized features within a spatially global kernel formulation.

The viscous Burgers experiment extends the numerical assessment to a nonlinear differential operator. At the investigated viscosity of \(\nu=0.01\), the continuum-feature mean kernel, analytical constraint embedding, and nonlinear residual minimization provide an accurate approximation of the developing internal transition. The two-stage predictor–corrector procedure combines residual-guided collocation enrichment with narrower prescribed global and local Gaussian kernel widths, producing substantial improvements over the coarse predictor. These results demonstrate the feasibility of extending CFKS to nonlinear PDEs without introducing finite Gaussian-RBF feature realizations. However, because both the collocation distribution and kernel scales are modified between stages, the individual contributions of these refinement mechanisms cannot be isolated from the present experiment. Further assessment across different nonlinear operators and parameter regimes is therefore needed.

The principal significance of CFKS lies in using the continuum-feature limit as a direct computational representation rather than solely as an asymptotic interpretation of a finite feature model. Analytical marginalization removes finite-feature sampling variability while preserving the connection to the underlying Gaussian-RBF representation. Nevertheless, the method retains prescribed Gaussian widths, bounded center distributions, collocation configurations, and regularization parameters, whose selection influences accuracy and conditioning. Moreover, CFKS inherits the dense matrix assembly and linear-algebra costs of global kernel methods, while nonlinear problems require additional iterative computations. The time-dependent experiments also highlight the computational expense associated with residual evaluation and slab-to-slab solution transfer. Future research will address scalable low-rank and iterative kernel formulations, efficient residual evaluation, conditioning-aware parameter selection, and localized or domain- decomposed extensions. Broader nonlinear benchmarks and systematic investigations of collocation and kernel-scale refinement will further clarify the accuracy, robustness, and computational limits of CFKS.

## A From finite features to the CFKS representer form

We briefly show how the CFKS representer form follows from the finite RBF feature model. Consider<tbc>

\(u_M(\mathbf{z})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\sum_{m=1}^M\beta_m\phi_{\theta_m}(\mathbf{z}),\) (52)

<tbc>and let \(\{\ell_i\}_{i=1}^N\) denote the selected PDE, boundary, and initial functionals. Define the finite feature matrix<tbc>

\(Z_{im}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\ell_i[\phi_{\theta_m}],\) (53)

<tbc>and the feature vector<tbc>

\(\varphi_M(\mathbf{z})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}\left[\phi_{\theta_1}(\mathbf{z})\cdots\phi_{\theta_M}(\mathbf{z})\right]^\top.\) (54)

<tbc>Then<tbc>

\(u_M(\mathbf{z})=\varphi_M(\mathbf{z})^\top\beta.\) (55)

<tbc>For a minimum-norm feature-space solution satisfying the discrete constraints, the coefficient vector lies in the range of \(Z^\top\) and may therefore be written as<tbc>

\(\beta=Z^\top\alpha,\) (56)

for some coefficient vector \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^N\). Substituting into the finite feature representation gives \(u_M(\mathbf{z})=\varphi_M(\mathbf{z})^\top Z^\top\alpha\)
\(=\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_j\left[\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^M\phi_{\theta_m}(\mathbf{z})\ell_j[\phi_{\theta_m}]\right].\) (57) Because \(\ell_j\) acts on the second argument, the term in brackets can be written as \(\ell_j^{\mathbf{z}^\prime} k_M(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}'_j),\) (58) where the empirical feature kernel is \(k_M(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}')=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^M\phi_{\theta_m}(\mathbf{z})\phi_{\theta_m}(\mathbf{z}').\) (59) Hence \(u_M(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_j\ell_j^{\mathbf{z}^\prime} k_M(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}'_j).\) (60) If the feature parameters are sampled from \(\rho(\theta)\), then as \(M\rightarrow\infty\), \(k_M(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}')\longrightarrow k_\rho(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}')=\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim\rho}\left[\phi_\theta(\mathbf{z})\phi_\theta(\mathbf{z}')\right].\) (61) Under the regularity conditions used in this work, the linear functionals may be interchanged with the expectation, so that \(\ell_j^{\mathbf{z}^\prime} k_M(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}'_j)\longrightarrow\ell_j^{\mathbf{z}^\prime} k_\rho(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}'_j).\) (62) The continuum-limit representation is therefore \(u_h(\mathbf{z})=\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_j\ell_j^{\mathbf{z}^\prime} k_\rho(\mathbf{z},\mathbf{z}'_j),\) (63) which is the CFKS representer form used in the main text. This derivation also shows that the finite feature coefficients \(\beta\) disappear from the continuum formulation: their effect is transferred to the constraint-space coefficients \(\alpha\) through the empirical Gram structure, while the sampled kernel _kM_ is replaced by the analytically evaluated continuum-feature mean kernel \(k_\rho\). ## B Analytical Derivation of the Bounded Continuum-Feature Gaussian Kernel This appendix derives the closed-form mean kernel associated with a continuum of Gaussian radial-basis-function features whose centers are uniformly distributed over a bounded interval. The full-line version of this construction is classical and yields a squared-exponential covariance; see, for example, Rasmussen and Williams \[8\]. Here we retain the finite center-support interval explicitly, which produces additional error-function terms. ### B.1 One-dimensional Gaussian feature model Consider the Gaussian feature \(\phi_c(x)=exp\left(-\frac{(x-c)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),\sigma>0,\) (64) where the center _c_ is distributed uniformly over \(c\sim\mathcal{U}[a,b],a

## B.2 Completion of the square Define the midpoint and separation coordinates \(m=\frac{x+y}{2},d=x-y.\) (68) We first rewrite the quadratic form in the exponent: \((x-c)^2+(y-c)^2=x^2+y^2-2c(x+y)+2c^2.\) (69) Using \(x^2+y^2=\frac{(x-y)^2}{2}+\frac{(x+y)^2}{2},\) (70) and \(2(c-m)^2=2c^2-2c(x+y)+\frac{(x+y)^2}{2},\) (71) we obtain \((x-c)^2+(y-c)^2=2(c-m)^2+\frac{(x-y)^2}{2}.\) (72) Substituting eq. 72 into eq. 67 gives \(k_{[a,b]}(x,y)=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{(x-y)^2}{4\sigma^2}\right)\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{(c-m)^2}{\sigma^2}\right)dc\)
\(=\frac{\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{d^2}{4\sigma^2}\right)}{b-a}\int_a^b\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{(c-m)^2}{\sigma^2}\right)dc.\) (73) Thus, the kernel separates into a Gaussian factor depending on the relative distance _d=x-y_ and a finite-support correction depending on the midpoint _m_=(_x+y)/_2. ## B.3 Evaluation using the error function Introduce the change of variables \(z=\frac{c-m}{\sigma},dc=\sigma dz.\) (74) The limits become \(z_a=\frac{a-m}{\sigma},z_b=\frac{b-m}{\sigma}.\) (75) Therefore, \(\int_a^b\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{(c-m)^2}{\sigma^2}\right)dc=\sigma\int_{z_a}^{z_b}e^{-z^2}dz.\) (76) Using the error function \(\mathrm{erf}(z)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{\pi}}\int_0^ze^{-t^2}dt,\) (77) we have \(\int_{z_a}^{z_b}e^{-z^2}dz=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{2}\left[\mathrm{erf}(z_b)-\mathrm{erf}(z_a)\right].\) (78) Hence, \(\int_a^b\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{(c-m)^2}{\sigma^2}\right)dc=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\sigma}{2}\left[\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{b-m}{\sigma}\right)-\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{a-m}{\sigma}\right)\right].\) (79) Substitution into eq. 73 yields the closed form \(\boxed{k_{[a,b]}(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\sigma}{2(b-a)}\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{(x-y)^2}{4\sigma^2}\right)}\)
\(\times\left[\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{b-\frac{x+y}{2}}{\sigma}\right)-\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{a-\frac{x+y}{2}}{\sigma}\right)\right].\) (80) Equation eq. 80 is the bounded continuum-feature Gaussian kernel used in this work.

## B.4 Interpretation of the bounded-support correction The expression in eq. 80 can be written schematically as \(k_{[a,b]}(x,y)=k_\mathrm{rel}(x-y)k_\mathrm{sup}\left(\frac{x+y}{2}\right),\) (81) where \(k_\mathrm{rel}(x-y)=\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{(x-y)^2}{4\sigma^2}\right)\) (82) depends only on the point separation, while \(k_\mathrm{sup}(m)=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\sigma}{2(b-a)}\left[\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{b-m}{\sigma}\right)-\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{a-m}{\sigma}\right)\right]\) (83) depends on the midpoint _m_=(_x+y)/_2. This decomposition shows explicitly why the bounded-center kernel is generally nonstationary. If the center support is finite, two pairs of points with the same separation _x-y_ can have different covariance if their midpoints lie at different distances from the center-support boundaries. Away from the edges _a_ and _b_, and provided the support is wide relative to \(\sigma\), the two error functions approach +1 and -1, respectively, so that the support correction becomes approximately constant. Near the edges, however, the finite-support correction modifies the kernel. ## B.5 Full-line limit The relationship with the standard Gaussian or squared-exponential kernel is obtained by taking \(a\rightarrow-\infty,b\rightarrow+\infty.\) (84) Since \(\mathrm{lim}_{z\rightarrow+\infty}\mathrm{erf}(z)=1,\mathrm{lim}_{z\rightarrow-\infty}\mathrm{erf}(z)=-1,\) (85) the bracketed factor in eq. 80 tends to 2. If one considers the unnormalized center measure \(d\mu(c)=dc,\) (86) rather than the uniform probability density 1/(_b-a_), the corresponding full-line feature integral is \(\widetilde{k}_\mathbb{R}(x,y)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty\phi_c(x)\phi_c(y)dc\)
\(=\sqrt{\pi}\sigma\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{(x-y)^2}{4\sigma^2}\right).\) (87) After normalization of the amplitude, this is a squared-exponential kernel with effective length scale \(\ell=\sqrt{2}\sigma,\) (88) under the conventional form \(k_\mathrm{SE}(x,y)=\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{(x-y)^2}{2\ell^2}\right).\) (89) Thus, the usual stationary Gaussian kernel is recovered as the infinite-support limit of the Gaussian center-feature construction, while the bounded-center model retains additional support information.

## B.6 Positive semidefiniteness The positive semidefiniteness of eq. 66 follows immediately from its feature representation. For arbitrary points \(\{x_i\}_{i=1}^N\) and coefficients \(\{\alpha_i\}_{i=1}^N\), \(\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N\alpha_i\alpha_jk_{[a,b]}(x_i,x_j)=\mathbb{E}_c\left[\sum_{i,j}\alpha_i\alpha_j\phi_c(x_i)\phi_c(x_j)\right]\)
\(=\mathbb{E}_c\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^N\alpha_i\phi_c(x_i)\right)^2\right]\ge 0.\) (90) Hence, the continuum-center construction defines a valid positive semidefinite kernel independently of the closed-form calculation. ## B.7 Differentiation of the mean kernel For PDE applications, the essential quantity is not only _k_[_a,b_](_x,y_) itself but its derivatives with respect to both arguments. Since the Gaussian feature and all of its derivatives are smooth, and the center support \[_a,b_\] is bounded, differentiation may be interchanged with integration: \(\partial_x^p\partial_y^qk_{[a,b]}(x,y)=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b\partial_x^p\phi_c(x)\partial_y^q\phi_c(y)dc.\) (91) Equation 91 gives a direct mean interpretation of every differentiated kernel block. For example, \(\partial_x\phi_c(x)=-\frac{x-c}{\sigma^2}\phi_c(x),\) (92) and \(\partial_x^2\phi_c(x)=\left[\frac{(x-c)^2}{\sigma^4}-\frac{1}{\sigma^2}\right]\phi_c(x).\) (93) Therefore, \(\partial_x\partial_yk_{[a,b]}(x,y)=\mathbb{E}_c\left[\partial_x\phi_c(x)\partial_y\phi_c(y)\right],\) (94) and similarly, \(\partial_x^2\partial_y^2k_{[a,b]}(x,y)=\mathbb{E}_c\left[\partial_x^2\phi_c(x)\partial_y^2\phi_c(y)\right].\) (95) For a differential operator L, \(\boxed{\mathcal{L}_x\mathcal{L}_yk_{[a,b]}(x,y)=\mathbb{E}_c\left[(\mathcal{L}\phi_c)(x)(\mathcal{L}\phi_c)(y)\right].}\) (96) Thus, the operator kernel used in the continuum-feature collocation method is precisely the mean Gram kernel of the operator-applied Gaussian features. ## B.8 Gaussian moment representation Higher-order derivatives can be evaluated efficiently without repeatedly differentiating the error-function expression eq. 80. After completing the square, every mixed derivative reduces to finite combinations of Gaussian moments of the form \(J_n(m)=\int_a^b(c-m)^nexp\left(-\frac{(c-m)^2}{\sigma^2}\right)dc.\) (97) The first moments are \(J_0=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\sigma}{2}\left[erf\left(\frac{b-m}{\sigma}\right)-erf\left(\frac{a-m}{\sigma}\right)\right],\) (98) and \(J_1=\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\left[exp\left(-\frac{(a-m)^2}{\sigma^2}\right)-exp\left(-\frac{(b-m)^2}{\sigma^2}\right)\right].\) (99)

For \(n\ge 2\), integration by parts gives the recursion \(J_n=-\frac{\sigma^2}{2}\left[(b-m)^{n-1}e^{-(b-m)^2/\sigma^2}-(a-m)^{n-1}e^{-(a-m)^2/\sigma^2}\right]+\frac{(n-1)\sigma^2}{2}J_{n-2}.\) (100) This recursion provides a convenient analytic route to the high-order kernel derivatives required by elliptic, advection- diffusion, and biharmonic operators. ### B.9 Extension to multiple dimensions Suppose the _d_-dimensional Gaussian feature is separable, \(\phi_\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})=\prod_{r=1}^d\mathrm{exp}\left(-\frac{(x_r-c_r)^2}{2\sigma_r^2}\right),\) (101) and the center coordinates are independently distributed as \(c_r\sim\mathcal{U}[a_r,b_r].\) (102) The mean density factorizes, \(\rho(\mathbf{c})=\prod_{r=1}^d\frac{1}{b_r-a_r},\) (103) and therefore the multidimensional kernel also factorizes: \(k_\rho(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\mathbb{E}_\mathbf{c}\left[\phi_\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})\phi_\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{y})\right]\)
\(=\prod_{r=1}^dk_{[a_r,b_r]}^{(r)}(x_r,y_r).\) (104) Consequently, mixed derivatives also factorize: \(D_\mathbf{x}^\alpha D_\mathbf{y}^\beta k_\rho(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\prod_{r=1}^d\partial_{x_r}^{\alpha_r}\partial_{y_r}^{\beta_r}k_{[a_r,b_r]}^{(r)}(x_r,y_r).\) (105) This property is particularly useful for Cartesian embedding domains and space-time formulations. For example, a two-dimensional Laplacian kernel can be assembled from one-dimensional derivative factors, while space-time advection-diffusion kernels can be constructed from separate spatial and temporal mean kernels. ### B.10 Summary The continuum-center Gaussian feature model therefore admits the exact bounded-support kernel \(k_{[a,b]}(x,y)=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}\sigma}{2(b-a)}e^{-(x-y)^2/(4\sigma^2)}\left[\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{b-\frac{x+y}{2}}{\sigma}\right)-\mathrm{erf}\left(\frac{a-\frac{x+y}{2}}{\sigma}\right)\right],\) (106) which reduces to a Gaussian/squared-exponential kernel in the full-support limit after normalization. More importantly for PDE collocation, the differentiated mean kernel satisfies \(D_x^\alpha D_y^\beta k_\rho(x,y)=\mathbb{E}_{c\sim\rho}\left[D_x^\alpha\phi_c(x)D_y^\beta\phi_c(y)\right].\) (107) Hence, the differential-operator kernel matrices used by the proposed method are exactly the continuum limits of the corresponding finite Gaussian-RBF operator Gram matrices. ## CRediT authorship contribution statement **Vikas Dwivedi:** Conceptualization, Methodology, Software, Writing - Original Draft, **Bruno Sixou** and **Monica Sigovan:** Supervision and Writing - Review & Editing.
